title: How it works
sub: From a task to a merged pull request, and where each step happens

noProject.text: Most buttons here open a project screen, so they wait until you add a project.

flow.lead: Every task takes the same path. Nothing in it starts, pushes or merges without your click.

project.title: Add a project
project.body: Open a folder, clone from GitHub or start an empty one. The setup steps pick its runners, accounts, caps and rules, and nothing is written until Create project.

task.title: Describe a task
task.body: Write what you want in the Tasks composer, with images or files if they help, or let the task assistant turn a conversation into drafts.

proposal.title: Get a crew proposal
proposal.body: Crewyard proposes who plans, implements, tests and reviews it: one tile per role with runner, model and account, a one-line reason and a cost estimate. Each role gets two standbys.

approve.title: Approve it
approve.body: Nothing starts until you press Approve and start. Before that you can change any role, profile, model or dependency; a changed pick is remembered as a preference.

worktrees.title: Agents work in worktrees
worktrees.body: Each code-writing run gets its own git worktree, so your checkout stays as it is. The project's tests run at every turn boundary and a failure goes back to the same session. Agents commit locally.

inbox.title: Answer in the Inbox
inbox.body: Agent questions, tool approvals and limit decisions wait there with a risk level. High-risk commands are approved one at a time, and a request you leave unanswered never turns into an approval.

review.title: Review the result
review.body: A reviewer on a different model checks the exact commit, and Ready for review is never shown as merged. Research, review and docs tasks end with a report of findings and suggested tasks.

ship.title: Push, PR and merge
ship.body: Branches wait in GitHub under Waiting to push until you click. A pull request is made only after the review gate passes and you click; a merge needs every gate and your approval.

checklist.lead: Read from this machine and your projects as they are now.
checklist.unknownHint: Crewyard could not read this right now.

machine.label: This machine can run tasks
machine.hint: Git and at least one agent CLI that Crewyard starts: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Gemini CLI.
machine.attention_one: Tasks can run. This machine still has {{count}} check that needs attention.
machine.attention_other: Tasks can run. This machine still has {{count}} checks that need attention.
machine.problem: Git is not installed, and tasks cannot run without it. Install Git, then press Check again on This machine.
machine.refused: Every agent CLI found is at a version Crewyard does not start: a Gemini CLI too old to keep profiles apart, or an OpenCode 2.x that has not passed its checks. This machine has the command that fixes it.

profile.label: A profile ready to run
profile.hint: A profile with a stored API key that was not refused, a runner sign-in that is signed in, or a local provider.
profile.problem: A key was refused or is not stored, or a sign-in needs a newer CLI.

project.label: A project open
project.hint: Open a folder or create a project from the Start screen.

firstTask.label: A first task
firstTask.hint: Describe one in the Tasks composer. Submitting it only opens the crew proposal.

firstCrew.label: A first approved crew
firstCrew.hint: Look over a crew proposal and press Approve and start.

github.label: GitHub connected
github.hint: Crewyard uses the GitHub CLI's own login (gh auth login) and stores no token of its own.
github.problem: The GitHub CLI (gh) was not found on this machine.

assistant.title: Task assistant and ready-made analyses
assistant.body: A read-only chat in the bottom panel that turns what you describe into task drafts.

points.a: It never edits files or starts runs. Add as draft gives a task whose crew still waits for you.
points.b: Six ready-made analyses (review, optimizations, bugs, security, dependencies and licences, test gaps) are local templates with no model call; up to three are suggested for the project.
points.c: Its spend counts against the profile key's daily cap and says Estimated. It stops on Stop and close or after sitting idle.

autopilot.title: Autopilot
autopilot.body: An opt-in mode of the task assistant, per project and off by default.

points.a: After a consent card it may create tasks, edit ones that have not started, approve their crews when the Estimated cost fits, retry a failed step once and cancel its own tasks.
points.b: Your limits: per task, per day, tasks per hour and tasks at once ($1.00, $5.00, 4 and 2 by default). Only your click changes them.
points.c: It can never push, open pull requests, merge, delete, spend past a cap, answer the Inbox or sign in. Stop Autopilot refuses everything at once without stopping running agents.

autopilot.go: Turn it on in the assistant

panel.title: Bottom panel
panel.body: One panel with five tabs: Assistant, Terminal, Events, Logs and Problems.

points.a: The terminal is your own shell in the project folder or a task's worktree. It starts only when you press New terminal and never gets an API key.
points.b: Problems lists every failure of the project in one place, each with a button to where you fix it.
points.c: Inside a project the panel never closes: its toggle, or Ctrl J, folds it to its tab strip and back. Folding stops nothing, the assistant included; closing a terminal's tab ends its shell after asking.

fallback.title: Fallback and handoff
fallback.body: When a limit or a credit runs out, each task follows its own rule.

points.a: Manual, the default, pauses and asks in the Inbox. Ask names the proposed standby, so one click continues. Auto moves to the next standby whose checks pass and tells you afterwards.
points.b: A handoff stops at a turn boundary, commits work in progress locally and gives the standby a package: goal, plan, diff, failing tests and open questions. Nothing is pushed.
points.c: Moving to another account of the same provider is a separate opt-in in Settings, off by default.

limits.title: Limits and where numbers come from
limits.body: Every quota or cost number carries one of these labels.

estimated.meaning: Crewyard computed it from tokens and catalog prices

unknown.meaning: no trustworthy source, never drawn as a percentage

plan.meaning: a subscription or a local model: tokens are counted, dollars are not

points.a: A window turns amber past 80% and red past 95%, with one notice each time.
points.b: Spend caps are per key and per task; a run stops and asks at the cap.

agentfiles.title: Your own agent files and skills
agentfiles.body: Settings lists the instructions, rules, skills, commands and subagents you wrote for each tool, without opening a key or settings file.

points.a: Share one with a profile, or with every profile of a runner: it is copied into that profile's own folder in the runner's format, never linked.
points.b: Scripts need a tick before they are copied, and a copy that is out of date waits for Sync.
points.c: A project's AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md can reach the runners that do not read it, per project and off by default.

crew.title: Editing the crew
crew.body: In the Crew graph every change is its own action; moving a node only changes the layout.

points.a: While it is a proposal: add or remove a step, change its role, profile or model, draw a depends-on edge and order the standbys.
points.b: While it runs: retry a failed step, skip one that has not started, pause or resume all, and add a follow-up step that waits for your approval.
points.c: Right-click a node, or press Shift F10, for every action, with the reason when one is off.

keyboard.title: Keyboard
keyboard.body: Every shortcut is declared once and listed in the keyboard map.

keys.q: Where do my API keys go?
keys.a: They are encrypted with Windows DPAPI and reach a runner only as an environment variable of its process. They never go on a command line, into a log, into git or into a URL, and agent shells and the terminal cannot see them.

nothingStarts.a: No crew starts before you press Approve and start, and pushes, pull requests, merges and spend past a cap always wait for your click. The one exception is Autopilot, which you turn on per project: it may approve crews of tasks it created within your limits, and it still never pushes or merges.

closePanel.q: Does closing a panel stop an agent?
closePanel.a: No. Closing the inspector or the window, or folding the bottom panel, keeps agents running, and the tray icon stays. Only two controls stop what they show, and they say so: the assistant's Stop and close, and a terminal's own close.

estimated.q: Why does a number say Estimated?
estimated.a: Crewyard computed it: tokens times the versioned catalog price, with the provider's own billing rules such as peak hours and paid web searches. Reported means the provider said it; Unknown means there is no trustworthy source, and it is never drawn as a percentage.

subscriptions.q: Does Crewyard read my subscription sign-ins?
subscriptions.a: No. Each CLI signs in through its own login inside the profile's own folder, and Crewyard never reads its tokens. Claude Code profiles use Anthropic API keys only.

release.q: Is this build signed, and does it update itself?
release.reading: Settings, under Updates, shows whether this build is signed and whether it looks for updates.
release.unsigned: Crewyard {{version}} is not code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher when you install it.
release.signed: Crewyard {{version}} is code-signed, and it installs only updates that Windows verifies as signed by its publisher.
release.feed: It looks for updates when you press Check now under Updates in Settings, or on its own once you turn on Check automatically. Downloading and installing always wait for your click.
